=== trail.py
trail.py: the trail of one entry of POSITIONS.md, from the repository's history.

    python3 -I trail.py 86            (or P-86)
    python3 -I trail.py 86 --short    the commit list only, one line each
    python3 -I trail.py 86 --at REV   the record as commit REV holds it

Prints:
  1. the entry's text at HEAD (for an entry struck from POSITIONS.md: STRUCK at the top, with the
     commit that removed it and the reason its history block gives, and the text as it last stood);
  2. its blocks in POSITIONS-history.md at HEAD, each with the commit that wrote it (the oldest
     commit whose history file holds the block's provenance line). A block's own "commit X" names
     the source it cites, not its writer;
  3. every commit that made or changed the entry's text, oldest first, read from each commit's own
     tree (side branches included): hash, UTC author time, subject, what it did, how the link to
     the text before was made (number, line, title: exact; similarity: score printed), how many
     other entries of POSITIONS.md the commit changed, and the reasons on record: the history
     blocks it wrote, the comments above verbatim copies of the text in the old history file, and
     the commit message.
  4. a cross-check: the old history lines that the numbering block names as earlier texts of this
     entry, and whether each is a text of this trail.

What a commit did:
  created          a text new in POSITIONS.md that no removed or earlier text explains
  changed          a text that replaced another of the same commit (link: number, line, title or similarity)
  moved to history the text left POSITIONS.md and stands verbatim in POSITIONS-history.md
  archived         a verbatim copy stored in POSITIONS-history.md by a later commit
  re-created       a text new in POSITIONS.md made from an earlier text (archived or removed)
  restored         a text back in POSITIONS.md verbatim from POSITIONS-history.md
  renumbered       the same text under a new number (2026-10-13: none -> P-n)
  struck           the number left POSITIONS.md (the first event of a struck entry's trail)
=== near.py
near.py: the curator's messages in a window before a UTC time, each with the coordinating
session's message that it answered, found along the transcript's reply chain.

    python3 -I near.py 2026-09-26T10:22:23Z            window 60 minutes before the time
    python3 -I near.py 2026-09-26T10:22:23Z 15m        or 2h, 1d
    python3 -I near.py 2026-09-26T10:22:23Z 15m --cut 2000
                                                        cut each printed text at 2000 characters
                                                        (his and the coordinator's), saying so;
                                                        by default every text is printed whole

For each message of his: its time, source (main, s1, queued: see show.py), session, length and
full text. Then the message he answered: the coordinator's turn that his message follows on the
reply chain (tlib.py says how the chain is read), every text of that turn whole, each with its
time and the file and line it was read from (the first copy, when a resumed transcript replays
it). Before it, one line for each turn the chain passed over as not addressed to him (replies to
Stop-hook feedback, to an agent's message or hand-back, to a task notification or check-in, to a
system reminder), and for each text written after he sent his message; a passed-over turn that
answers a notification and ends with an ask to him (a question mark, "The ask", "I recommend",
"your yes", ...) is marked, and the newest such turn printed whole, since he may have answered
it. When he quotes lines ("> ..."), the text on the chain that holds them is named, and printed
whole if it is not the answer. After it, the last lines of the three turns to him further back
on the chain, for a message that answers an older question. A queued message (sent while a turn
ran) starts at its delivery into the turn; texts written after he sent it are not taken. A
message on no chain the index holds (a queued one never delivered) falls back to the time: the
coordinator's last text before it, passing over replies to Stop-hook feedback.

=== later.py
later.py: his messages after an entry's creation that may bear on it, though no commit of the
entry followed them (his later word may have gone into a skill or another record instead).

    python3 -I later.py 148                   (or P-148)
    python3 -I later.py 148 --top 25          how many to print (default 15)
    python3 -I later.py 148 --at 36f7db77c --until 2026-10-21T20:54
                                              the entry's text at a commit, and no message after a time

The candidates are his messages in the coordinating sessions (tlib.COORDINATING) from the entry's
creation on (for an entry struck from POSITIONS.md, its last text is read, and the list runs on
past the removal) (the first commit of its trail that made its text), less those that leads.py already
printed near the entry's own commits. Each is scored by the entry's distinctive terms:
  - its title's words, beyond common words (a stop list, and words in more than a tenth of his
    messages), lightly stemmed (possessive and plural off, cut to 7 letters); each weighs its
    rarity in his messages, log(messages / messages holding it);
  - its names in backticks, weight 3 each.
A term in his own words (lines that do not start with ">") counts whole; a term only in the
exchange around his message (the coordinator's message he answered, by the reply chain, its
reply to him, and the lines he quoted) counts half. A message also gains 8 when it falls in the
30 minutes before a commit that changed a file the entry names in backticks (`compiler.md`), other
than the entry's own commits, in lines that hold a title term (3 when the lines hold none): that
is where his word may have gone. Naming the entry's number (P-148, or as dictated, P148) adds 8 in
his words, 2 in the exchange. A message is a candidate when its weight is at least 5 (MIN) and it
holds a term in his own words or falls before such a commit. Printed: rank, weight, time, whether it
is after the entry's last change, the terms (in parentheses when only in the exchange), the commit
it precedes, and its first 300 characters; then how many candidates there were in all.

=== quote.py
quote.py: does the curator's message at a UTC time hold a quote word for word?

    python3 -I quote.py "QUOTE" 2026-09-26T10:21:32Z
    python3 -I quote.py "QUOTE" 2026-09-26T10:21        a prefix: every message of his in that minute

The time is a prefix of his message's timestamp, as show.py takes it (a trailing Z is dropped).
For each message of his at that time it prints one verdict:
  EXACT        the quote is a substring of the message as stored
  NORMALISED   a substring once both have every run of whitespace made one space, ends trimmed,
               and the curly apostrophe U+2019 made a straight one (nothing else is changed)
  NO MATCH     neither; it then prints the longest run of the quote's words that the
               message holds word for word (after the same normalising), for a reader to judge
With the match it prints the message's text around it.

=== pointers.py
pointers.py: every line of the record that names an entry of POSITIONS.md by its number.

    python3 -I pointers.py 86            (or P-86)
    python3 -I pointers.py 86 --at REV   the files as commit REV holds them

Searches, at the working tree: explorations/coordinator/FACTS.md, POSITIONS.md, PLAN.md,
review-queue.md, HELD.md and BOOT.md; explorations/reviews/open-asks-*.md; and every file under
.claude/skills/. The history files (POSITIONS-history.md, FACTS-history.md) are not searched:
trail.py reads the first, and both only record. A line counts when it holds the number as a word:
P-86 matches, as in "P-86's" or "(P-86)", but P-860 and P-186 do not. A line that names a range
holding the number ("P-85 to P-88") is listed too, marked as a range.
Prints path:line and the line (cut at 400 characters around the number; --whole prints it whole),
grouped by file; the entry's own line in POSITIONS.md is marked.

=== homes.py
homes.py: where a status that an entry of POSITIONS.md states may already live.

    python3 -I homes.py 151            (or P-151)
    python3 -I homes.py 151 --top 8    candidates per sentence (default 5)
    python3 -I homes.py 151 --at REV   the three files as commit REV holds them

Splits the entry (the working tree's POSITIONS.md; for an entry struck from it, its text as it
last stood, said so at the top) into sentences, and a sentence into its clauses
at the semicolons outside parentheses; a clause keeps the label that opens its sentence, as
"Built:" or "Still to build:". A clause states a status when it, its label or its sentence holds
one of the status words: built, to build, landed, pending, default, waits, standing go, listed for his
review, open, held, parked, owed, taken, stands at, returns after, not moved, and the like.

For each such clause it lists the candidates that may already hold the same point: the numbered
items of review-queue.md's lists (b) and (c), and the lines of PLAN.md (a numbered sub-line also
carries its parent's item number, and its own number as a fork when the parent counts forks).
A candidate is listed when it names the entry or shares a distinctive term with the clause:
  row N, item N (PLAN's), review-queue item N, fork N, way N, batch N, rung X, phase N, ask N,
  decision X, another entry's P-N, a name in backticks (a commit hash too), a dotted finding
  name such as judge-review.1 or A.skeptic.2
Each shared term weighs by its rarity among the candidates (log of the candidates over those
holding it); naming the entry adds 2; content words shared (four letters or more, beyond common
words) add a little, to order near-ties, and are printed apart. Candidates are ranked by that
weight, and each is printed with what it shares, for the scout to confirm or reject.

=== comments.py
comments.py: his saved page comments that bear on an entry of POSITIONS.md.

    python3 -I comments.py 66            (or P-66)

He also comments on pages, and those comments are not in the transcripts. They are saved as
explorations/coordinator/positions-audit/evidence/curator-comments-*.md: a section per thread,
headed "## On <what it was anchored to>", with one bullet per comment, "- HH:MM: "words"".
A section counts when its heading, or a comment counts when its own words, either
  - name the entry's number, also as dictated: P-66, P66, PE66, P 66 (not P-660), or
  - quote its title: a quoted run ("..." or curly quotes) of at least three content words, at
    least 60 % of which are words of the entry's bold title (case, possessives and punctuation
    ignored).
A section that counts is printed whole, with its heading; a comment that counts in another
section is printed with that section's heading. Each with its file and line.

=== hischeck.py
hischeck.py: check the block of his quotes that a scout's or reader's report ends with.

    python3 -I hischeck.py FILE...

Each FILE holds a block headed "## His quotes" (to the next "## " heading or the end), one line
per quote of his:
    HIS 2026-09-26T10:21:32.097Z | Run Fable judgement as well.
(a line may be wrapped in backticks or start with "- "). The time is a prefix of his message's
timestamp, as show.py takes it (a trailing Z dropped); each message of his at that time is tried,
and the quote is checked as quote.py does:
  EXACT        a substring of the message as stored
  NORMALISED   a substring once whitespace is collapsed and U+2019 made a straight apostrophe
  NO MATCH     neither, in every message at that time (quote.py "QUOTE" TIME shows the nearest run)
  NO MESSAGE   no message of his at that time
Lines of the block that start with HIS but do not parse are counted as BAD FORM. Prints, per
file, the counts and every line that is not EXACT or NORMALISED, with its line number; exits 1
when any line fails or a file has no block.

    python3 -I show.py 2026-10-12T15:53:07.5     # a finer prefix
    python3 -I show.py --list 2026-10-12         # one line per message (timestamp, source, length, start)
    python3 -I show.py --count                   # how many messages the three sources give

<!-- Review written 2026-09-26 by a delegated worker session, for Pavol: in what form the revised specification shows that the revival changed a passage, and where the original text and the reasoning live. Built fresh from Specification/, its build, its git history and peer language specifications; the revival's planning notes on this question were not read. No other file in the tree was changed, and no PDF was built. -->

# How a revival change should show in the specification

## The question, and the words used

The revival will change a rule of the language. The compiled type checker keeps the
*multiple instantiation exclusion*: a type may not be a subtype of two different
instantiations of one generic type (for example, of both `List⟦ZZ32⟧` and `List⟦String⟧`).
Some sentences of the specification, the language definition kept as LaTeX sources in
`Specification/` (the "July 2012 draft"), allow exactly that, and some of its examples rely
on it. Those sentences will be edited. The question here is only the *form* of that edit:
how the rebuilt `Specification/fortress.pdf` shows that a passage was changed by the
revival, and where the original wording and the reasoning are kept.

Pavol's requirement (2026-09-24), split into the five things it asks for:

- **D1** "update the spec with the change that we do";
- **D2** "somehow properly record why we decided that way";
- **D3** "no open discrepancy between the spec and our implementation that would be confusing to people";
- **D4** "preserve the original historic record somewhere in a document with our reasoning why we did the switch";
- **D5** "preserve the option to go the route C".

*Route C* is not defined in the brief. I read it as the route that keeps the
specification's permission and makes the implementation support a type extending two
instantiations. If that reading is wrong, only the wording of the route-C remarks in § 8
changes, not the costs.

Two words recur. *Normative* text is the text that defines the language: a program is
right or wrong by it. *Informative* text explains and binds nothing. Standards put
informative material in *annexes*, which are appendices of a standard.

------
### 9. The options, as they would be put to Pavol

1. **The specification's own way, layered as in 1.0 and 2009.**
   - Edit the normative sentences in place.
   - At each changed passage, a labelled callout that prints in both builds: a new macro,
     not `\note`, so it is not taken for the authors' remarks.
   - In Appendix I, a new section, "Changes made by the 2026 revival to the working draft",
     one entry per change. Each entry has C++'s four fields (affected section, change,
     rationale, effect) and two more: the original text, quoted verbatim with its path and
     line in `Specification-1.0-frozen/`, and the alternative not taken (route C), with what
     reversing to it would take.
   - One paragraph in the front-matter figure (`preamble.tex`), and a changed title-page
     line.
   - The full reasoning in a repository document, cited by the entry.
   - Optionally, route C as an entry in Proposed Features, next to the team's own note at
     `internal-document.tex:363`.

   It commits him to: one small macro; an appendix that must be kept up to date with every
   later revival change (the one place the team let decay); one repository document per
   decision; and a PDF rebuild, which every form needs anyway.

2. **Steele's CLtL2 way.** Keep the original sentences in place, marked as outdated by a
   dotted margin rule. Print the new sentences with a solid rule and a paragraph "The revival
   decided on 2026-09-24 to ...". Number each decision into an index at the end, and explain
   the convention in the front matter. It commits him to: the `changebar` package, untested
   with this document; a PDF that prints both wordings; readers who must learn the
   convention; and keeping both wordings coherent under later edits. In exchange, the original
   stays visible in place and reversing to route C is a swap of the rules.

3. **The Ada way.** One source, two PDFs: a clean normative build, and an annotated build with
   inserted and deleted text marked and a reason beside each change. It commits him to:
   reworking the release switch (today it also hides the implementation-status boxes), a first
   release build, and two committed PDFs to keep in step.

4. **Keep the history outside, the Java and Python way.** Edit in place with no mark in the
   PDF. The original text, reasoning and route C go in a repository document and the commit
   message, and the frozen copy holds the original wording. It commits him to nothing in the
   build, and to a PDF that cannot tell its reader that a rule changed or why.

What decides between them is how much of D2, D4 and D5 must be readable in the PDF itself,
without the repository. Options 1 and 2 carry all three in the PDF, option 3 carries them in
the second PDF, and option 4 carries none. Between 1 and 2 the choice is whether the original
wording should sit in the appendix (quoted once, in the entry) or in the body (printed beside
the new rule).

My reading, not a decision: option 1. It is the specification's own form (its empty Appendix I
and its front matter, used as the team used them for 1.0), it keeps the original wording
inside the PDF as well as in the untouched frozen copy, and the route-C entry states what
reversing it would take.

5:## 1. The list, written before any edit
11:1. `Specification/basic/trait-parameters.tex:339-351` (E1, the covariance example): "Trait declarations are allowed to extend other instantiations of themselves", `trait C[\S\] extends C[\T\] where {S extends T, T extends Object}`, "we have expressed the fact that the static parameter S of C is covariant". States the rule's opposite (`:339-340`) and its example is refused. Verdict: judgement section 3.1, E1, option 1: kept as "Not allowed", with the library's widening function with bounded static parameters as the way (`Library/CovariantCollection.fss:15-36`); the callout carries the one sentence on the `covariant` modifier (`POSITIONS.md:147`). Frozen: `Specification-1.0-frozen/basic/trait-parameters.tex:339-351`.
13:3. `Specification/basic/trait-parameters.tex:383-399` (E3, the `Empty` list): `object Empty extends List[\T\] where {T extends Object}`. Refused. Verdict: section 3.1, E3, option 1: kept as "Not allowed", with `object Empty[\T\] extends List[\T\]` beside it. Frozen: same file, `:383-399`.
14:4. The where-clause section as a whole, `Specification/basic/trait-parameters.tex:284-399`: one new sentence, that a where-clause variable may not appear as a static argument in an `extends` clause (judgement sections 5 and 7).
50:## 2. The rule as the revision states it

# The specification

Three folders hold the team's specification:

- `Specification/` is the team's text, as the revival revises it. It says what the language means, except where a decision of the curator says otherwise.
- `Specification-1.0-frozen/` is the unrevised copy. Cite it as "the Working Draft of February 2011". Only `fortress.1.0.pdf` in it is the 1.0 release. Leave this copy unchanged.
- `Documentation/Specification/` is the team's later restart, which they did not finish. If its Types chapter, `Documentation/Specification/Prose/Language/types.tick`, covers a topic, cite it beside `Specification/` as the designers' later word.

Appendix I, `Specification/appendices/changes.tex`, records the changes to the text. Its revival section has one entry for each change that the revival made.

A draft build prints the team's `\note{}` boxes, and a release build hides them. Many say that a feature was not built, for example "Reduction variables are not yet supported." Before you record a missing feature as a gap, grep the notes of its chapter: `grep -n '\\note{' Specification/<file>.tex`.

The api listings of the library part are generated from the library's `.fsi` files when the specification is built (`Specification/library/apis/`, not in the tree). A listing shows the library itself, so it cannot justify a change of the library. Cite the `.fsi` file.

To weigh the specification against the team's later texts, or to find the designers' reason for a rule, read `exploring.md`, "Weighing the sources".

## Changing the text: the revision form

Every change of the text has the four parts below, so that no disagreement between the text and an implementation stays hidden.

1. An entry in the revival section of Appendix I: a `\subsection` with a `\seclabel`. The entry gives:
   - the affected sections, the change, its rationale and its effect. The effect names each departure: each way in which walk or the compiled path does not do what the new text says, with its ledger row.
   - the original text, quoted with its path and line in `Specification-1.0-frozen/`;
   - what a reversal to the alternative not taken would need;
   - the decision of the curator that it follows (its POSITIONS entry), or the reason that your brief gives.

   For the form, print one entry, about 2 KB: `explorations/coordinator/tools/facts-extract.sh 'doc:Specification/appendices/changes.tex#choice of a coercion'`.

2. At each changed passage, a callout that prints in every build, unlike a `\note`:

       \revision{<label>}{<what changed, in a sentence or two>}

   `<label>` is the `\seclabel` of the entry. `Specification/fortress/fortress.tex` defines `\revision`.

3. The front matter's one paragraph on the revision, in `Specification/fortress/preamble.tex`. If your change makes it false, correct it.

4. The full reasoning, in `decision-record.md` in the folder of your work under `explorations/`: each changed passage, the original and the new text, the reason, and the way back. For the form, print one passage of an earlier record, about 4 KB: `explorations/coordinator/tools/facts-extract.sh 'doc:explorations/compile-ladder/rung-spec-route-a/decision-record.md#3.3'`.

If the revision refuses an example, keep the example in the text, marked "Not allowed", as the specification itself does. If your change contradicts a calculus of Appendix A, keep the calculus's rules and soundness claims. Add a callout to it that says what it predates.

Check each changed sentence of `Specification/` or `Documentation/` against the curator's decisions. If it says what walk or the compiled path does, run a program that shows it.

## Building it

To check your LaTeX, build the specification in a built tree, after the setup lines. It takes about 90 s, so start it detached (`session.md`, "Long commands"):
-----
# What the revival changed in the team's Fortress

The team left three forms of Fortress, which disagree in places:

- the specification;
- walk, with the interpreter's library;
- the compiled path, with the compiler's library.

This part lists each change of the revival made for one of two reasons: two of the team's sources contradict each other, or a program failed. Its headings are the points of `SKILL.md`, "Fortress as a language", that the changes qualify.

Each resolution is the rule of this tree. Follow it as you follow a decision of the curator, and question it only on new evidence (`SKILL.md`, "When to explore"). Where it changed the specification, Appendix I keeps the original text (`specification.md`). The Working Draft is the unrevised specification, in `Specification-1.0-frozen/`. `exploring.md`, "Weighing the sources", describes the type group, whose later texts most resolutions follow.

If a source of the team's, an old note or your training disagrees with this skill, find the point below. Search for the construct's name: a change that fits no heading, such as walk's `if`, stands under the nearest one. If it is there, follow the skill: it describes the tree. If it is not, do as `SKILL.md`, "When to explore", says.

A note written before the revival, and your training, can be right about the team's walk and out of date here. Three examples: the number types form a tower, fixed-width arithmetic wraps, and walk converts no argument.

### 5. What the team already did when it revised the text

- **For a release (2008).** The 1.0 PDF opens with a front-matter statement of where and why
  it departs from 1.0β ("to synchronize the specification with the implementation", page 2)
  and ends with Appendix F, "Changes between Fortress 1.0 β and 1.0 Specifications" (pages
  259-260). Appendix F is a short-form changes annex. Its bullets are: features "temporarily
  dropped" to match the implementation (16 listed); libraries changed; syntax and semantics
  changed, each with its chapter or section number; features added; features eliminated.
  It gives no reason per item. Neither the internal appendix nor the "not yet supported"
  boxes appear in the 1.0 PDF's text, which fits a release build.
- **For the working draft (2009).** Sukyoung Ryu re-imported the sources part by part
  (`3ac302f43` to `0f49d8698`, 2009-10-19 to 11-06), "The next task is to integrate the
  technical decisions since 1.0." She then added the list of features not yet implemented
  (`61e28a78c`) and "the technical decisions since F1.0beta and the issues to discuss"
  (`93f5018fd`, 27 files, 39 note lines added and 6 removed, Proposed Features rewritten).
  Those decisions went in as draft notes at the passage, often dated and attributed:
  "We require a dotted field access by a “self.” prefix. (08/11/08) -- Sukyoung"
  (`basic/traits.tex:310`), "Resolve ambiguity in favor of longest API name. (07/23/09)"
  (`basic/components/intro.tex:99`). Reviewers' remarks went in as notes and margin notes
  (`178405db2`, 14 notes and 8 margin notes), and a proposal went into Proposed Features
  (`3f89470e5`).
- **For corrections.** The team edited in place, with no mark, and gave the credit in the
  commit message: "Clarification suggested by Nels Beckman" (`9ced3777d`, Victor Luchangco,
  `advanced/overloading.tex`). Once the old sentence was kept as a LaTeX comment beside the
  new one (`44e03b176`).
- **Before a large revision (2012).** Steele copied the whole directory to
  `Specification-1.0-frozen/` (`c02fa44d0`) and, four months later, began a new document
  instead of editing the old one (way 13). The copy's name suggests the 1.0 text, but it is
  not that. `git diff 2f8b4331a:Specification c02fa44d0:Specification-1.0-frozen` is empty,
